say.text: A 46-year-old woman attends the outpatient clinic with two days of right upper abdominal pain, a fever of 38.4 °C and a positive Murphy's sign.
Her bloods are pending. Which imaging test do you order first?

choices.label: CT scan of the upper abdomen
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the question's key word. Is it asking for the test that comes first at the bedside, or the most accurate test once the picture is clear?
Yes. Ultrasound is the initial test for gallstones and suspected acute cholecystitis: quick, bedside and highly sensitive for stones.
It shows wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign, which help confirm the picture.
That choice is not right.
HIDA is tempting: it is the most accurate test for acute cholecystitis.
This question asks for the first test, and accuracy answers a different question.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so split the two words: 'first' asks for the initial test, 'most accurate' asks for the confirming test.

say.text: That choice is not right.
CT feels thorough, so it is tempting as the first look at a sick gallbladder.
But CT misses many gallstones and is kept for complications such as perforation or abscess.

sure_note.text: You were sure: CT answers the complications question, not the first gallbladder test.

say.text: Ultrasound is equivocal in a septic post-operative patient. You need a test that confirms cystic duct obstruction.
Which finding, on which test, makes the diagnosis?

choices.label: Wall thickening and fluid around the gallbladder on repeat CT
Gallbladder not filling while tracer reaches the duodenum on HIDA
Dilated bile duct with a stone seen on MRCP
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of a radionuclide test that follows bile from the liver into the gut. Ask whether the gallbladder fills on the way.
Yes. HIDA is the most sensitive and specific test. Gallbladder non-filling, with tracer in the duodenum, confirms cystic duct obstruction.
The gallbladder ladder is now clear: ultrasound first, HIDA when the picture stays unclear, and CT for complications.
That choice is not right.
Repeat CT is tempting, because it does show the inflamed wall, though it is not the test of choice here.
This question asks which test shows the cystic duct is blocked. That is a tracer finding, not a wall finding.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a picture of inflammation is not proof that the cystic duct is blocked.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A dilated duct with a stone looks decisive, and MRCP is a real test for duct stones.
But this question is about the cystic duct at the gallbladder neck, which shows on the gallbladder's own tracer study.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a bile-duct picture answers a bile-duct question, not this one.

say.text: A 61-year-old man is jaundiced. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a dilated common bile duct.
You want to confirm a duct stone without a procedure. What do you order next?

choices.label: Diagnostic ERCP as the first step
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Focus on the phrase 'without a procedure'. Which test images the bile ducts from outside the body?
Yes. MRCP is the non-invasive investigation of choice for common bile duct stones.
Ultrasound and HIDA look at the gallbladder, so they cannot settle the duct question. Duct questions climb to the duct tests.
That choice is not right.
Repeat ultrasound is tempting, because it found the gallstones and feels like the test for the whole tree.
But ultrasound is the gallbladder test. The duct question needs a duct test such as MRCP.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the test that found gallbladder stones is not automatically the duct test.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Diagnostic ERCP is tempting: it sees the duct directly, and it can also treat what it finds.
But a non-invasive test answers the question first. ERCP is kept for a stone already found and due for removal.

sure_note.text: You were sure: ERCP is diagnostic and therapeutic, so it belongs after a duct stone is found.

say.text: Which is the non-invasive investigation of choice for common bile duct stones?

choices.label: CT scan of the upper abdomen

say.text: Yes. MRCP is non-invasive and detects common bile duct stones well.
ERCP answers the same duct question with an endoscope, so it is kept for treatment once a stone is found. EUS helps with small stones.
That choice is not right.
CT is tempting: it images the whole abdomen and sometimes shows a dilated duct.
But CT misses many gallstones and is kept for complications.

sure_note.text: You were sure: CT is the complications test, not the duct test.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Ultrasonography is tempting: it is the first test in every gallstone work-up.
But the question asks about the duct, and ultrasound is the gallbladder test.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the first gallbladder test is not the duct test.

say.text: That choice is not right.
ERCP is tempting: it is the duct test with the most power, because it can also treat.
But the question asks for the non-invasive test, and ERCP passes an endoscope into the duct.

sure_note.text: You were sure: ERCP is the treatment step, so it follows the non-invasive test.

say.text: Now the TG18 criteria. Which combination makes a suspected diagnosis of acute cholecystitis?

choices.label: One local sign, one systemic sign and imaging
Stones on ultrasound plus one local sign
Two systemic signs, such as fever and high CRP
One local sign plus one systemic sign

say.text: Yes. Suspected needs one local sign (A) and one systemic sign (B).
Imaging (C) is added only to reach a definite diagnosis: A plus B plus C.
That choice is not right.
Imaging feels necessary, since pictures are the most objective part of the work-up.
But imaging is the third item and upgrades a suspected case to definite. It is not part of suspected.

sure_note.text: You were sure: imaging belongs to the definite set, not the suspected one.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Stones on ultrasound feel like proof, so one local sign plus the picture seems enough.
But suspected needs a systemic sign as well. The picture only counts once the clinical pair is present.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a stone on the scan is the third item, which needs the clinical pair before it counts.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Fever and a raised CRP are real inflammation, so two systemic signs feel convincing.
But the set must include a local sign (A). Two systemic signs without one do not make suspected.

sure_note.text: You were sure: systemic signs are the B item, and the set always needs an A item too.

say.text: A 55-year-old man has fever and a positive Murphy's sign. No imaging has been done yet.
At which TG18 level does he sit now?

choices.label: Definite, since the signs look strong
Not diagnosable until imaging is done
Not yet suspected, needs a second local sign
Suspected, with the signs he has so far

say.text: That choice is not right.
Definite feels right because the signs look serious.
But definite needs the imaging item as well, and he has none yet.

sure_note.text: You were sure: definite is A plus B plus C, so it waits for the picture.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Waiting for imaging feels careful, since the diagnosis is confirmed by pictures.
But imaging is needed only to reach definite. The clinical items already set the first level.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the clinical items come first, and the picture only upgrades them.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A strict rule feels safer, since the local sign is the core of the disease.
But TG18 pairs one local sign with one systemic sign. A second local sign is not part of the rule.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the rule is one A item and one B item, not two A items.

say.text: Yes. One local sign and one systemic sign make a suspected diagnosis. Imaging upgrades it to definite.
Read the TG18 set as a sequence: local and systemic signs first, then the picture to confirm.
